language_wrapper: On a circular street with {n_houses} labeled houses, the mail carrier plans a delivery pattern for a single day under these rules: (i) no two adjacent houses receive mail on the same day, and (ii) there are never more than {max_no_mail_run} consecutive houses in a row that receive no mail on that day. If exactly {deliver_count} houses receive mail, how many distinct labeled delivery patterns are possible around the circle?
hardness_rationale: The seed counts linear binary strings with local constraints (no adjacent ones, and no three consecutive zeros). Here, we generalize to circular strings (wrap-around constraints) with an exact number of ones and a variable maximum zero-run length. Circular constraints couple the first and last positions, requiring careful accounting of merged zero-runs across the boundary. Imposing an exact count of ones further complicates the combinatorics, ruling out simple recurrences that ignore global totals. The intended solution uses a stateful dynamic programming (or transfer-matrix/generating function) approach with memory that tracks the trailing zero-run, the presence and length of the leading zero-run up to the first one, and the ones count. This is materially more involved than the seed’s single-parameter recurrence and is robustly resistant to guessing.
notes: Proof sketch: Model the day’s pattern as a binary string of length n arranged on a cycle. Let L be the max allowed consecutive zero run. We must count strings with exactly k ones subject to (i) no adjacent ones and (ii) every zero-run length is at most L, including the run that may straddle the boundary between position n and 1. Split into two disjoint cases: Case A, b1=1, and Case B, b1=0. Case A: The boundary between positions n and 1 contains at least one 1, so the zero-runs on either side do not merge across wrap-around. Hence we can count open strings b2..bn by DP tracking the last bit, current zero-run z, and ones count w, with the final step constrained to set bn=0. Case B: b1=0. Let lead_z be the length of the initial zero-run (until the first 1 occurs). Track a flag indicating whether the first 1 has been seen; before the first 1, we have prev=0 and lead_z=z; after the first 1, lead_z is fixed, and we propagate with prev in {0,1}, current zero-run z, and ones count w. At the end, the wrap-around zero-run is exactly lead_z + z_end and must be ≤ L; adjacency across the boundary is automatically satisfied because b1=0. Summing the counts from both cases yields the total number of labeled circular patterns. Feasibility requires 2k ≤ n ≤ k(L+1), since with k ones on a cycle there are exactly k zero-runs, each in [1, L]. The DP enumerations are exact because they are derived from the defining local constraints with the only global coupling handled explicitly at the boundary (bn relative to b1 in Case A and the merged zero-run in Case B).
source_question: A mail carrier delivers mail to the nineteen houses on the east side of Elm Street.  The carrier notices that no two adjacent houses ever get mail on the same day, but that there are never more than two houses in a row that get no mail on the same day.  How many different patterns of mail delivery are possible?
